q: A sled slides down a straight slope. Why does the normal force of the snow do no work on the sled, although it is a large force?
a: The normal force is perpendicular to the slope and so to the motion of the sled. Only the component of the force along the motion does work, $W = F_\parallel s$, and for the normal force it is zero. The normal force does act indirectly, however, because the kinetic friction is $\mu N$.

q: When do you choose the equation of motion and when the work–energy principle? Give one example of each from the situations of this chapter.
a: The equation of motion $\Sigma\overline{F} = m\overline{a}$ fits when the question is about a force or an acceleration at some moment, for example the reading of a scale in an accelerating lift. The work–energy principle fits when the question is about the speed at some point or the change in energy over a distance, for example the speed of a sled at the foot of a slope. In both you start from the free-body diagram.

q: Why does the horizontal distance from the top to the stopping point of a sled starting from rest not depend on the mass of the sled?
a: The work $mgh$ done by the weight and the work $-\mu mgx$ done by friction are both proportional to the mass. In the work–energy principle $mgh - \mu mgx = 0$ the mass cancels, and $x = h/\mu$, when the coefficient of friction is the same all the way and air resistance is ignored.
